system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

Division of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery
Angioplasty/Stent Discharge Instructions

Medications:
Take Aspirin 325mg (enteric coated) once daily 
If instructed, take Plavix (Clopidogrel) 75mg once daily
Continue all other medications you were taking before surgery, 
unless otherwise directed
You make take Tylenol or prescribed pain medications for any 
post procedure pain or discomfort

What to expect when you go home:
It is normal to have slight swelling of the legs:
Elevate your leg above the level of your heart (use ___ 
pillows or a recliner) every ___ hours throughout the day and at 
night
Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated
It is normal to feel tired and have a decreased appetite, your 
appetite will return with time 
Drink plenty of fluids and eat small frequent meals
It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber, 
lean meats, vegetables/fruits, low fat, low cholesterol) to 
maintain your strength and assist in wound healing
To avoid constipation: eat a high fiber diet and use stool 
softener while taking pain medication

What activities you can and cannot do:
When you go home, you may walk and go up and down stairs
You may shower (let the soapy water run over groin incision, 
rinse and pat dry)
Your incision may be left uncovered, unless you have small 
amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing or 
band aid over the area that is draining, as needed
No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 lbs) for 
1 week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications
Call and schedule an appointment to be seen in ___ weeks for 
post procedure check and ultrasound 

What to report to office:
Numbness, coldness or pain in lower extremities 
Temperature greater than 101.5F for 24 hours
New or increased drainage from incision or white, yellow or 
green drainage from incisions
Bleeding from groin puncture site

SUDDEN, SEVERE BLEEDING OR SWELLING (Groin puncture site)
Lie down, keep leg straight and have someone apply firm 
pressure to area for 10 minutes. If bleeding stops, call 
vascular office ___. If bleeding does not stop, call 
___ for transfer to closest Emergency Room. 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

no pleural effusions or pneumothorax.  Minimal degenerative changes are seen
within the thoracic spine.

IMPRESSION:  No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the vascular surgery team. You've been admitted because we're concerned about a narrowing in the artery that supplies blood to your transplanted kidney on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had high blood pressure lately—could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s one of the main clues. When the artery to a transplanted kidney narrows, it often causes worsening or hard-to-control hypertension. Your recent ultrasound suggested this might be the case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now? Are they going to operate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We plan to do a minimally invasive procedure called an angiogram tomorrow. We’ll go through your groin to look at the artery with imaging, and if we confirm the narrowing, we’ll place a small stent to open it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I mean, with my kidney function and everything…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. Because your kidney function is borderline, we’ll use carbon dioxide instead of regular contrast dye during the procedure. It’s safer for your kidneys and reduces the risk of further damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under light sedation—relaxed and drowsy, but not fully asleep. The procedure usually takes about an hour. You’ll go to the recovery area afterward and stay overnight for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable. What about my other meds? I take a lot for my transplant and diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue most of them. We’ll hold your furosemide and lisinopril tomorrow morning until we check your kidney function after the procedure, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll still take your Lantus at night and use Humalog as needed based on your blood sugar checks. We’ll monitor that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want my sugars going wild.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep them in check. For now, we’re starting IV fluids to hydrate you well before the procedure—that helps protect your kidneys too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable—creatinine is 1.8, which is about your baseline. We’re on track for your procedure this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Nervous, but ready to get it done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally normal. The team is ready, and we’ll be with you the whole time. Any last questions before we take you to the OR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—what if the stent doesn’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The success rate is high. Most patients see improvement in blood pressure and kidney function. If it recurs later, there are other options, but we’ll cross that bridge if we come to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Great news—procedure went perfectly. We confirmed a significant narrowing in the artery to your transplanted kidney, placed a stent, and now blood flow looks excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Did you use the CO2 like you said?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we did—minimal contrast, so your kidneys were protected. You’re back on the floor now, and we’ll keep an eye on your groin site and kidney values.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. A little sore in the groin, but not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll give you some pain medication if you need it. Keep your leg straight for a few hours to let the puncture site heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep you through tomorrow so we can check your labs in the morning and make sure there are no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your creatinine is stable at 1.8, and your blood pressure is already better—138 over 76 on your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. You’re doing well. I’ll go over your discharge instructions and meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, what about the new medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your transplant and diabetes meds. We’re adding a daily aspirin and clopidogrel—Plavix—to keep the stent open and prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already on Plavix. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, perfect. Just keep taking it daily. Also, take the pain medication as needed, but only until the soreness goes away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not while you’re taking the pain pills. Once you’re off them, you can resume driving. Also, no heavy lifting—nothing over five pounds—for at least a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about showering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower today—just let the water run over the groin site, then pat it dry. No soaking in a tub yet. If there’s any drainage, cover it with a bandage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your kidney doctor and our vascular team in two weeks. They’ll check your kidney function and do an ultrasound to make sure the stent is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have fever, increasing pain or swelling in the leg, numbness, or bleeding from the groin. If there’s sudden, severe bleeding, lie down, keep your leg straight, and have someone press firmly on the site for ten minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, Doctor. I feel a lot better knowing what to expect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be home within the hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll make that follow-up call today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of a right renal transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, was admitted for evaluation and treatment of right renal artery stenosis. He presented with progressive hypertension, and a renal artery duplex suggested stenosis. He was admitted for preoperative hydration and underwent a successful CO2-guided renal arteriogram and stent placement the following day. The procedure was uncomplicated, and his kidney function remained stable postoperatively. He was discharged home the next day in stable condition with instructions to continue immunosuppressive, antihypertensive, and antiplatelet therapies, and to follow up with renal and vascular clinics in two weeks.
